Delegation and token exchange
Last reviewed 2026-10-01 · Jump to reference

Objective. After this module you can tell delegation from impersonation in a token, name the three parameters RFC 8693 requires and the four it leaves to you, enforce who is allowed to act for whom, and say what an exchange does not fix.

Before you start. Every module so far has assumed the caller is the party doing the work. An agent is not. It holds a token that came from somewhere else and it calls on behalf of a person who is nowhere in the request.
Published lesson 20 of 27Complete the lesson and quick check, then record your progress.
Learn
1. The attack

Running example: a travel assistant agent calling ExampleAir's booking API for a signed-in traveller. Company names are fictional. The traveller's own token carries five scopes. The agent needs one of them, bookings:write, for one booking.

There are four ways that call gets made in practice, and three of them are the attack. The agent can forward the traveller's token untouched. It can use its own standing service credential and mention the traveller in a request parameter. It can exchange the token for one that claims to be the traveller. Or it can exchange it for one that says an agent is calling for the traveller, which is the only shape that lets the booking service decide correctly.

What makes this worth a module is that the first three look identical in a design document and identical in a dashboard. They differ in exactly one place: what the downstream service can tell about who is calling. OWASP files the consequences as ASI03 Identity & Privilege Abuse in the Top 10 for Agentic Applications, released December 2025, and puts the mechanism plainly: "Leaked credentials let them operate far beyond their intended scope".

The downstream service wants to knowPassthroughService credentialDelegation token
Which user is this forThe userNot in the tokenThe user
Which agent is callingNot in the tokenThe agentThe agent
How much authority came with itAll five scopesWhatever the service holdsOne scope
Can I apply an object checkYesNo, no user to check againstYes
Who to suspend if the agent misbehavesOnly the userThe service, and every caller of itThat agent
What a stolen copy reachesEverything the user can doEverything the service can doOne scope, one audience

The service-credential row is the confused deputy, and it is the one that survives review most often, because it looks like good hygiene: the agent has its own identity and its own credential. It does. The problem is that the traveller has left the request, so module 9's object check has nothing to compare the booking against.
2. Why it works
Impersonation and delegation are different, and the specification says so

RFC 8693, published January 2020, defines one new grant type for token exchange, urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange, and spends its first section separating two things people say interchangeably.

Impersonation: "When principal A impersonates principal B, A is given all the rights that B has within some defined rights context and is indistinguishable from B in that context." Indistinguishable is the operative word. Nothing downstream can tell an agent did this.

Delegation: "With delegation semantics, principal A still has its own identity separate from B, and it is explicitly understood that while B may have delegated some of its rights to A, any actions taken are being taken by A representing B."

In the protocol the difference is one request parameter. Send subject_token alone and you are asking for impersonation. Send actor_token as well and you are asking for delegation, and the token that comes back carries an act claim naming the actor. Checks 3 and 4 of the lab are that one parameter, and checks 7 and 8 are what the booking service writes in its log as a result.
Three required parameters, and four decisions nobody makes for you

Section 2.1 marks exactly three parameters REQUIRED: grant_type, subject_token and subject_token_type. One more is conditional: actor_token_type "is REQUIRED when the actor_token parameter is present in the request but MUST NOT be included otherwise", which is why checks 14 and 15 of the lab are both refusals.

audience, resource, scope and requested_token_type are all OPTIONAL. Nothing in the specification caps the lifetime of the issued token either. Read that as a list of four decisions that are yours, because the specification will not stop you issuing a token that is broader and longer-lived than the one you were handed. The lab's Part D is those four, each with the policy on and off: check 27 shows a client omitting scope and receiving all five of the traveller's scopes, and check 35 shows a server handing out an hour on the strength of a token with five minutes left.

Section 5 is three paragraphs long and the third one is the design advice: "Any time one principal is delegated the rights of another principal, the potential for abuse is a concern. The use of the scope claim (in addition to other typical constraints such as a limited token lifetime) is suggested to mitigate potential for such abuse, as it restricts the contexts in which the delegated rights can be exercised."
may_act, and the one MUST on reading the result

Two JWT claims carry this. The act claim goes in the issued token and names the current actor. may_act goes in the subject token and names who is allowed to become one: "The may_act claim makes a statement that one party is authorized to become the actor and act on behalf of another party." It is how the traveller's token says which agent may act for the traveller, decided when that token was issued rather than at the moment an agent asks.

Match it on issuer and subject together. A sub is only unique within an issuer, so an agent registered somewhere else can hold the same sub as yours, which is check 24 of the lab.

Chains nest. "A chain of delegation can be expressed by nesting one act claim within another. The outermost act claim represents the current actor while nested act claims represent prior actors." And then the sentence that decides how your resource server reads it: "For the purpose of applying access control policy, the consumer of a token MUST only consider the token's top-level claims and the party identified as the current actor by the act claim."

That MUST exists because the obvious implementation violates it. Given a nested chain and a list of allowed actors, walking the chain until something matches feels tolerant and reads as defensive coding. It means any service that ever appears in a chain can act through any service that comes after it. Checks 38 and 39 are the same token read both ways, and they disagree.
The whole system
Something the service cannot tellBoth parties stated
3. The control

1. Exchange, do not forward. A user token that leaves the service it was issued for is a credential with no stated holder. If the agent needs to call downstream, it exchanges.
  2. Send actor_token. Delegation is one parameter more than impersonation and it is the parameter that makes the log useful.
  3. State audience and scope on every exchange, and refuse the request at the authorization server when they are missing. The default of copying the subject token's scope is the worst one available.
  4. Enforce may_act, matched on issuer and subject together, so the subject token decides which agents may act for it.
  5. Cap the issued lifetime at what remains on the subject token, and shorter where the task is short.
  6. Read the token the way section 4.1 requires: top-level claims plus the current actor, and nothing else in the chain.
  7. Log both parties. Every downstream decision records the subject and the current actor, because an incident needs to know which agent to suspend without suspending the user.
  8. Bind the issued token to its holder where the threat model warrants it, with the mechanisms from module 8. An exchange adds no binding of its own.
4. Defaults and when to change them

DecisionStarting defaultChange it when
How an agent calls downstreamDelegation, with actor_tokenImpersonation only where the downstream service must not learn an agent exists, and then say so in writing.
Forwarding the user's tokenNeverNo exception. The token's audience says who it was for.
scope on the exchangeRequired, and the narrowest the task needsRFC 8693 makes it optional. Your server should not.
audience or resourceRequired, one target per exchangeA token with no audience is a token every service has to decide about on its own.
Issued lifetimeCapped at the subject token's remaining life, and shorter for short tasksLonger only where a task genuinely outlives its trigger, and then with a refresh path rather than a long token.
may_actEnforced, matched on issuer and subjectMatching sub alone is the bug. Matching nothing means any registered agent can act for any user.
Reading a delegation chainCurrent actor onlyNever. Section 4.1 states it as a MUST.
Chain depthBounded, and the bound is smallA chain long enough to be interesting is usually a design you can shorten instead.
Holder binding on the issued tokenAdded separately where it mattersThe exchange will not do it. Bearer is the default you get.
5. What it proves, and what it doesn't

Proves: that the downstream service knows which agent is calling and which user it is for, that the authority travelling with the call is the authority the task needs, and that an agent acting for a user was one the user's token permitted.

Doesn't prove: that the agent is doing what the user asked. A delegation token is a correct answer to "may this agent act for this user, here, now". It says nothing about whether the booking is the one the traveller wanted, which is later in Part 4.

An exchange is not a revocation boundary. Check 40 of the lab revokes the traveller's token and the next exchange is refused. Check 41 takes the token that was issued a moment earlier and it still works, for the full 300 seconds it was granted, because nothing links the two. Short lifetimes are the control here, not revocation lists.
6. Prove it

• A list of every path where a service calls another service on a user's behalf, and which of the four shapes each one uses.
  • No path on that list forwards a token outside the audience it was issued for.
  • Every exchange in the code states audience and scope, verified by reading the calls rather than the design.
  • The authorization server refuses an exchange with no scope stated, and the refusal is tested.
  • The authorization server enforces may_act on issuer and subject, and the test includes a same-sub agent from another issuer.
  • Issued lifetimes are capped at the subject token's remaining life, with the cap tested.
  • Resource servers authorize on the current actor only, with a test that a prior actor in a nested chain does not grant access.
  • Access logs carry both the subject and the current actor for every delegated call.
7. Exercise
Download labs/token_exchange_lab.py. It needs nothing beyond Python 3.

There is no python3 command on a default Windows install, so use py -3 there. The tokens are real HS256 JWTs, minted with hmac, compared with hmac.compare_digest and decoded with json. Checks 1 to 4 are the module in four lines. Three of the four shapes print the same identity twice, and each one is missing a different half of the answer. Only line 4 names both parties, and the difference between line 3 and line 4 is one request parameter.

Checks 9 and 10 are the same comparison measured as blast radius. The forwarded token reaches all five of the traveller's operations. The delegated one reaches the single scope it was issued for. Neither number is a property of the protocol; the second one is a property of the request the agent chose to make, which is why check 27 matters: omit scope and you are back to five.

Part C is worth running twice. Check 22 refuses an exchange because the traveller's token names no authorized actor, and check 23 is the same request to a server that does not look, which issues it. Both servers are implementing RFC 8693 correctly, because the specification never tells you to check. Check 24 is the version of this that gets through review: an agent with the right sub and the wrong issuer.

Checks 38 and 39 are the one place the specification makes the decision for you. The chain is traveller to assistant to pricing service to seat-map service. The seat-map service is not an allowed actor on the booking service, so reading the current actor refuses the call. Walking the chain finds the assistant three levels down and allows it. Section 4.1's MUST is there to forbid the second one.

Part F is the honest accounting. The exchange refuses to mint anything new from a revoked token, and the token minted thirty seconds before revocation keeps working until it expires. There is no cnf claim, so the issued token is a bearer token like any other: the exchange narrowed what the token can do and did nothing about who can present it.

Try next:

  • Set require_may_act=False on the main server and rerun. Three checks fail, and they are the three that decide whether an agent can act for a user who never said it could.
  • Change the resource server's chain walk to stop after one level instead of all of them. Decide whether that is a fix or a smaller version of the same bug.
  • Add a fifth hop to Part E and print the chain. Decide what depth you would refuse at, and what you would do with a token that exceeded it.
  • On the line that sets ttl, replace min(want_seconds, left) with want_seconds and rerun. Two checks fail, 34 and 43, and the token it issues outlives the session it came from.
  • For a service you work on: list the paths where it calls another service on a user's behalf, and mark which of the four shapes each one is. The ones you cannot classify are the finding.
8. Check your understanding

What is the protocol difference between impersonation and delegation?

One request parameter. An exchange with subject_token alone asks for impersonation, and RFC 8693 says the result is "indistinguishable from B in that context". Adding actor_token, with actor_token_type, asks for delegation, and the issued token carries an act claim naming the actor. The downstream service can then authorize the agent and attribute the action to the user.

Your agent has its own client credentials and calls the booking API with them, passing the user's ID as a parameter. What is wrong with that?

The user is not in the token, so the booking service has nothing to compare the requested booking against. Any object check it performs is checking against a user ID supplied by the caller, which is module 9's first trap. The token's authority is also the service's, not the user's, so it is the same for every user the agent serves.

A resource server receives a token with a nested chain of actors and finds an allowed service three levels down. May it allow the call?

No. RFC 8693 section 4.1 states that for applying access control policy the consumer MUST only consider the token's top-level claims and the party identified as the current actor. Allowing on a prior actor means any service that has ever appeared in a chain can act through any service that follows it.

You revoke a user's session. What happens to the delegated tokens already issued from it?

Nothing, unless you built something that links them. The exchange refuses to issue more, and the ones already out keep working until they expire. That is why the issued lifetime is a control rather than a detail, and why capping it at the subject token's remaining life is the starting default.

attrs.data-correct-feedback: Correct. The act claim is the whole difference: the downstream service can authorize the agent and still attribute the action to the user.
attrs.data-incorrect-feedback: Not quite. All four tokens verify and all four can carry a narrow scope. Only the delegation token names the agent as the current actor and the user as the subject, which is what lets the downstream service decide and attribute separately.

Quick check

What delegation adds

An agent calls the booking service for a signed-in traveller. Which property does only a delegation token give the booking service?

Exercises

Change one thing and predict the output

Each exercise edits one place in labs/token_exchange_lab.py and asks what the run prints. The answers are the real output of each variant, and where a variant changes nothing the answer carries the measurement from a request the lab does not make.

1. may_act is matched on the subject alone

In AuthorizationServer.exchange, replace the two-line test that compares the iss and sub of may_act with the iss and sub of the actor. Compare the subject only:

if allowed.get("sub") != actor.get("sub"):
Which check changes?

Every option, and why
  • The agent in check 21 has a different sub, https://other.exampleagent.example. A comparison on sub alone still refuses it, so check 21 stays invalid_request.
  • Only check 24 moves. Check 21 differs from the authorized actor in its sub, which is the one field the loosened test still reads.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 24 goes from invalid_request to issued. The agent from https://id.attacker.example carries the same sub as the traveller's assistant, and with the issuer dropped from the comparison nothing tells them apart. It now holds a delegation token for the traveller. Check dlg-05 in the Reference layer asks for issuer and subject together, and for this exact case in the test.
  • The lab signs every token with the same key, so the lookalike's token verifies. The comparison of may_act is the only thing that refuses it in check 24, and this edit is what loosens it.

2. Walking the chain becomes the default

In ResourceServer.__init__, change the default walk_chain=False to walk_chain=True. Nothing else changes, and no call site is edited.

Which check changes?

Every option, and why
  • In check 8 the current actor is the assistant, which is on the allowed list. The service allows the call before it reaches the chain walk, so the line still reads allowed, https://assistant.exampleagent.example for traveller-8812.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 38 goes from refused: https://seats.exampleair.example is not an allowed actor to allowed, https://seats.exampleair.example for traveller-8812 on a prior actor. The booking service in check 38 is built without stating walk_chain, so it takes whatever the default is. The seat-map service is still not an allowed actor. It gets in because the assistant appears further down the chain as a prior actor. Checks 38 and 39 now print the same line, which is the reading that check dlg-03 in the Reference layer says to test against.
  • Check 39 builds its resource server with walk_chain=True written out, so the default never applied to it. Its line is identical.
  • Check 38 moves, check 7 does not. The impersonation token has no act claim, so the service returns allowed, caller is traveller-8812 before any actor logic runs.

3. The lifetime cap is off by default

In AuthorizationServer.__init__, change the default cap_lifetime=True to cap_lifetime=False. The traveller's token still has 300 seconds left, and no exchange in the lab states how long it wants.

Which checks fail?

Every option, and why
  • Check 34 does fail, and it is not alone. Check 43 reads the exp claim of the same token, so it moves with it.
  • Check 35 already prints 3600 in the published lab. Its server is built with cap_lifetime=False written out, so the default never applied to it.
  • Check 44 still prints refused: expired. It presents the token at the token's own exp, whatever that is, so it is refused under either default.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures: check 34 goes from 300 to 3600, and check 43 goes from 300 to 3600. Check 33 still says the traveller's token has 300 seconds left. The exchange asked for nothing unusual: 3600 seconds is the request's default, and the cap was the only thing holding it to what the subject token had left. The token that survives revocation in check 41 is now usable for 3600 seconds, not 300. Check dlg-06 in the Reference layer is this cap.

4. The server stops insisting on a target

In AuthorizationServer.__init__, change the default require_target=True to require_target=False, so an exchange that names neither audience nor resource is no longer refused.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Correct. Exit 0, 61 of 61 lines identical. Every exchange the lab sends to a server built with the defaults names an audience, so the flag is never consulted. Measured on a request the lab does not make, the delegation exchange from check 20 with audience left out: as published the main server answers invalid_request, and with the default flipped it answers issued, with aud on the token set to None. The lab's booking service refuses that token with refused: wrong audience, so the damage depends on every resource server making that comparison. A passing run told you nothing here, because no check sends the request. Check dlg-04 in the Reference layer asks for the refusal at the authorization server.
  • Check 30 names a target, https://bookings.attacker.example. A named target the server does not know is still refused with invalid_target. The flag only matters when no target is named at all.
  • Check 32 already prints None in the published lab. Its server is built with require_target=False written out, so its line is identical.
  • Check 31 presents a token whose audience is the booking service. The payments service compares aud with its own name and still prints refused: wrong audience. This edit is at the authorization server and does not touch that comparison.

Reference
Controls
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

• StandardToken exchange uses the grant type urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange. RFC 8693 section 2.1.
  • StandardImpersonation makes the actor "indistinguishable from B in that context"; delegation keeps A's own identity and records that "any actions taken are being taken by A representing B". RFC 8693 section 1.1.
  • Standardgrant_type, subject_token and subject_token_type are REQUIRED. actor_token_type "is REQUIRED when the actor_token parameter is present in the request but MUST NOT be included otherwise". RFC 8693 section 2.1.
  • Standardaudience, resource, scope and requested_token_type are OPTIONAL, and no lifetime limit is specified. RFC 8693 section 2.1.
  • StandardThe response carries access_token, issued_token_type and token_type as REQUIRED; scope is "OPTIONAL if the scope of the issued security token is identical to the scope requested by the client; otherwise, it is REQUIRED". RFC 8693 section 2.2.1.
  • Standard"If the issued token is not an access token or usable as an access token, then the token_type value N_A is used." RFC 8693 section 2.2.1.
  • StandardAn invalid request, or a subject_token or actor_token that is invalid or "unacceptable based on policy", MUST return the invalid_request error code; invalid_target SHOULD be used when the server is unwilling or unable to issue for the requested target, and "other error codes may also be used, as appropriate". RFC 8693 section 2.2.2, with the error response format and codes from RFC 6749 section 5.2.
  • Standard"The outermost act claim represents the current actor while nested act claims represent prior actors." RFC 8693 section 4.1.
  • Standard"For the purpose of applying access control policy, the consumer of a token MUST only consider the token's top-level claims and the party identified as the current actor by the act claim." RFC 8693 section 4.1.
  • StandardThe may_act claim "makes a statement that one party is authorized to become the actor and act on behalf of another party", and helps the authorization server decide whether the requested delegation is permitted. RFC 8693 section 4.4.
  • Standard"The use of the scope claim (in addition to other typical constraints such as a limited token lifetime) is suggested to mitigate potential for such abuse, as it restricts the contexts in which the delegated rights can be exercised." RFC 8693 section 5.
  • StandardLeaked or over-broad agent credentials let an agent "operate far beyond their intended scope". OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, ASI03 Identity & Privilege Abuse.
  • BaselineExchange rather than forward. A user's token does not leave the audience it was issued for.
  • BaselineSend actor_token, so the downstream decision and the audit record name the agent and the user separately.
  • BaselineRequire audience and scope on every exchange at the authorization server, rather than defaulting to the subject token's scope.
  • BaselineEnforce may_act, matched on issuer and subject together.
  • BaselineCap the issued lifetime at the subject token's remaining life.
  • BaselineAuthorize on the current actor only, and bound the depth of chains you accept.
  • BaselineLog the subject and the current actor on every delegated call.
  • OptionBind the issued token to its holder with the mechanisms in module 8 where a stolen bearer token is in the threat model.
  • OptionIssue impersonation tokens where a downstream service must not learn that an agent is involved, recording the decision and accepting that attribution is lost.
  • OptionKeep an exchange record per issued token, so a revoked session can be traced to the tokens minted from it even though it cannot recall them.
Review checklist items
These are collected into the site checklist.

• No service forwards a user's token outside the audience it was issued for Verified by reading the outbound calls. A forwarded token carries all of the user's authority and names no agent.
  • Calls made on a user's behalf carry the user in the token, not in a parameter Otherwise the object check compares against a user ID the caller supplied.
  • Resource servers authorize on the current actor only RFC 8693 section 4.1 states it as a MUST. Test that a prior actor in a nested chain does not grant access.
  • Every exchange states audience and scope, and the server refuses without them Both are OPTIONAL in the specification. Defaulting to the subject token's scope copies everything.
  • may_act is enforced, matched on issuer and subject together A sub is unique only within an issuer. Include a same-sub, different-issuer case in the test.
  • Issued lifetimes are capped at the subject token's remaining life Nothing in RFC 8693 caps it. A revoked session cannot recall tokens already minted from it.
  • Delegation chain depth is bounded And the bound is small enough that exceeding it is a design question rather than an alert.
  • Access logs record the subject and the current actor separately An incident needs to suspend one agent without suspending the user.
Sources

• RFC 8693: OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange, January 2020. Sections 1.1, 2.1, 2.2.1, 2.2.2, 3, 4.1, 4.4 and 5.
  • RFC 6749: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework, October 2012. Section 5.2, the token endpoint error response and its error codes.
  • OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, OWASP GenAI Security Project, released 9 December 2025. ASI03 Identity & Privilege Abuse.

sections.heading: 2. Why it works
sections.html:
Impersonation and delegation are different, and the specification says so

RFC 8693, published January 2020, defines one new grant type for token exchange, urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange, and spends its first section separating two things people say interchangeably.

Impersonation: "When principal A impersonates principal B, A is given all the rights that B has within some defined rights context and is indistinguishable from B in that context." Indistinguishable is the operative word. Nothing downstream can tell an agent did this.

Delegation: "With delegation semantics, principal A still has its own identity separate from B, and it is explicitly understood that while B may have delegated some of its rights to A, any actions taken are being taken by A representing B."

In the protocol the difference is one request parameter. Send subject_token alone and you are asking for impersonation. Send actor_token as well and you are asking for delegation, and the token that comes back carries an act claim naming the actor. Checks 3 and 4 of the lab are that one parameter, and checks 7 and 8 are what the booking service writes in its log as a result.

Three required parameters, and four decisions nobody makes for you

Section 2.1 marks exactly three parameters REQUIRED: grant_type, subject_token and subject_token_type. One more is conditional: actor_token_type "is REQUIRED when the actor_token parameter is present in the request but MUST NOT be included otherwise", which is why checks 14 and 15 of the lab are both refusals.

audience, resource, scope and requested_token_type are all OPTIONAL. Nothing in the specification caps the lifetime of the issued token either. Read that as a list of four decisions that are yours, because the specification will not stop you issuing a token that is broader and longer-lived than the one you were handed. The lab's Part D is those four, each with the policy on and off: check 27 shows a client omitting scope and receiving all five of the traveller's scopes, and check 35 shows a server handing out an hour on the strength of a token with five minutes left.

Section 5 is three paragraphs long and the third one is the design advice: "Any time one principal is delegated the rights of another principal, the potential for abuse is a concern. The use of the scope claim (in addition to other typical constraints such as a limited token lifetime) is suggested to mitigate potential for such abuse, as it restricts the contexts in which the delegated rights can be exercised."

may_act, and the one MUST on reading the result

Two JWT claims carry this. The act claim goes in the issued token and names the current actor. may_act goes in the subject token and names who is allowed to become one: "The may_act claim makes a statement that one party is authorized to become the actor and act on behalf of another party." It is how the traveller's token says which agent may act for the traveller, decided when that token was issued rather than at the moment an agent asks.

Match it on issuer and subject together. A sub is only unique within an issuer, so an agent registered somewhere else can hold the same sub as yours, which is check 24 of the lab.

Chains nest. "A chain of delegation can be expressed by nesting one act claim within another. The outermost act claim represents the current actor while nested act claims represent prior actors." And then the sentence that decides how your resource server reads it: "For the purpose of applying access control policy, the consumer of a token MUST only consider the token's top-level claims and the party identified as the current actor by the act claim."

That MUST exists because the obvious implementation violates it. Given a nested chain and a list of allowed actors, walking the chain until something matches feels tolerant and reads as defensive coding. It means any service that ever appears in a chain can act through any service that comes after it. Checks 38 and 39 are the same token read both ways, and they disagree.

The whole system

Something the service cannot tellBoth parties stated

sections.heading: 3. The control
sections.html:
1. Exchange, do not forward. A user token that leaves the service it was issued for is a credential with no stated holder. If the agent needs to call downstream, it exchanges.
  2. Send actor_token. Delegation is one parameter more than impersonation and it is the parameter that makes the log useful.
  3. State audience and scope on every exchange, and refuse the request at the authorization server when they are missing. The default of copying the subject token's scope is the worst one available.
  4. Enforce may_act, matched on issuer and subject together, so the subject token decides which agents may act for it.
  5. Cap the issued lifetime at what remains on the subject token, and shorter where the task is short.
  6. Read the token the way section 4.1 requires: top-level claims plus the current actor, and nothing else in the chain.
  7. Log both parties. Every downstream decision records the subject and the current actor, because an incident needs to know which agent to suspend without suspending the user.
  8. Bind the issued token to its holder where the threat model warrants it, with the mechanisms from module 8. An exchange adds no binding of its own.

sections.heading: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.heading_text: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.html:
Proves: that the downstream service knows which agent is calling and which user it is for, that the authority travelling with the call is the authority the task needs, and that an agent acting for a user was one the user's token permitted.

Doesn't prove: that the agent is doing what the user asked. A delegation token is a correct answer to "may this agent act for this user, here, now". It says nothing about whether the booking is the one the traveller wanted, which is later in Part 4.

An exchange is not a revocation boundary. Check 40 of the lab revokes the traveller's token and the next exchange is refused. Check 41 takes the token that was issued a moment earlier and it still works, for the full 300 seconds it was granted, because nothing links the two. Short lifetimes are the control here, not revocation lists.

sections.heading: 6. Prove it
sections.html:
• A list of every path where a service calls another service on a user's behalf, and which of the four shapes each one uses.
  • No path on that list forwards a token outside the audience it was issued for.
  • Every exchange in the code states audience and scope, verified by reading the calls rather than the design.
  • The authorization server refuses an exchange with no scope stated, and the refusal is tested.
  • The authorization server enforces may_act on issuer and subject, and the test includes a same-sub agent from another issuer.
  • Issued lifetimes are capped at the subject token's remaining life, with the cap tested.
  • Resource servers authorize on the current actor only, with a test that a prior actor in a nested chain does not grant access.
  • Access logs carry both the subject and the current actor for every delegated call.

sections.heading: 8. Check your understanding
sections.html:
What is the protocol difference between impersonation and delegation?

One request parameter. An exchange with subject_token alone asks for impersonation, and RFC 8693 says the result is "indistinguishable from B in that context". Adding actor_token, with actor_token_type, asks for delegation, and the issued token carries an act claim naming the actor. The downstream service can then authorize the agent and attribute the action to the user.

Your agent has its own client credentials and calls the booking API with them, passing the user's ID as a parameter. What is wrong with that?

The user is not in the token, so the booking service has nothing to compare the requested booking against. Any object check it performs is checking against a user ID supplied by the caller, which is module 9's first trap. The token's authority is also the service's, not the user's, so it is the same for every user the agent serves.

A resource server receives a token with a nested chain of actors and finds an allowed service three levels down. May it allow the call?

No. RFC 8693 section 4.1 states that for applying access control policy the consumer MUST only consider the token's top-level claims and the party identified as the current actor. Allowing on a prior actor means any service that has ever appeared in a chain can act through any service that follows it.

You revoke a user's session. What happens to the delegated tokens already issued from it?

Nothing, unless you built something that links them. The exchange refuses to issue more, and the ones already out keep working until they expire. That is why the issued lifetime is a control rather than a detail, and why capping it at the subject token's remaining life is the starting default.

sections.heading: Change one thing and predict the output
sections.heading_text: Change one thing and predict the output
sections.html:
Each exercise edits one place in labs/token_exchange_lab.py and asks what the run prints. The answers are the real output of each variant, and where a variant changes nothing the answer carries the measurement from a request the lab does not make.

1. may_act is matched on the subject alone

In AuthorizationServer.exchange, replace the two-line test that compares the iss and sub of may_act with the iss and sub of the actor. Compare the subject only:

if allowed.get("sub") != actor.get("sub"):
Which check changes?

Every option, and why
  • The agent in check 21 has a different sub, https://other.exampleagent.example. A comparison on sub alone still refuses it, so check 21 stays invalid_request.
  • Only check 24 moves. Check 21 differs from the authorized actor in its sub, which is the one field the loosened test still reads.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 24 goes from invalid_request to issued. The agent from https://id.attacker.example carries the same sub as the traveller's assistant, and with the issuer dropped from the comparison nothing tells them apart. It now holds a delegation token for the traveller. Check dlg-05 in the Reference layer asks for issuer and subject together, and for this exact case in the test.
  • The lab signs every token with the same key, so the lookalike's token verifies. The comparison of may_act is the only thing that refuses it in check 24, and this edit is what loosens it.

2. Walking the chain becomes the default

In ResourceServer.__init__, change the default walk_chain=False to walk_chain=True. Nothing else changes, and no call site is edited.

Which check changes?

Every option, and why
  • In check 8 the current actor is the assistant, which is on the allowed list. The service allows the call before it reaches the chain walk, so the line still reads allowed, https://assistant.exampleagent.example for traveller-8812.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 38 goes from refused: https://seats.exampleair.example is not an allowed actor to allowed, https://seats.exampleair.example for traveller-8812 on a prior actor. The booking service in check 38 is built without stating walk_chain, so it takes whatever the default is. The seat-map service is still not an allowed actor. It gets in because the assistant appears further down the chain as a prior actor. Checks 38 and 39 now print the same line, which is the reading that check dlg-03 in the Reference layer says to test against.
  • Check 39 builds its resource server with walk_chain=True written out, so the default never applied to it. Its line is identical.
  • Check 38 moves, check 7 does not. The impersonation token has no act claim, so the service returns allowed, caller is traveller-8812 before any actor logic runs.

3. The lifetime cap is off by default

In AuthorizationServer.__init__, change the default cap_lifetime=True to cap_lifetime=False. The traveller's token still has 300 seconds left, and no exchange in the lab states how long it wants.

Which checks fail?

Every option, and why
  • Check 34 does fail, and it is not alone. Check 43 reads the exp claim of the same token, so it moves with it.
  • Check 35 already prints 3600 in the published lab. Its server is built with cap_lifetime=False written out, so the default never applied to it.
  • Check 44 still prints refused: expired. It presents the token at the token's own exp, whatever that is, so it is refused under either default.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures: check 34 goes from 300 to 3600, and check 43 goes from 300 to 3600. Check 33 still says the traveller's token has 300 seconds left. The exchange asked for nothing unusual: 3600 seconds is the request's default, and the cap was the only thing holding it to what the subject token had left. The token that survives revocation in check 41 is now usable for 3600 seconds, not 300. Check dlg-06 in the Reference layer is this cap.

4. The server stops insisting on a target

In AuthorizationServer.__init__, change the default require_target=True to require_target=False, so an exchange that names neither audience nor resource is no longer refused.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Correct. Exit 0, 61 of 61 lines identical. Every exchange the lab sends to a server built with the defaults names an audience, so the flag is never consulted. Measured on a request the lab does not make, the delegation exchange from check 20 with audience left out: as published the main server answers invalid_request, and with the default flipped it answers issued, with aud on the token set to None. The lab's booking service refuses that token with refused: wrong audience, so the damage depends on every resource server making that comparison. A passing run told you nothing here, because no check sends the request. Check dlg-04 in the Reference layer asks for the refusal at the authorization server.
  • Check 30 names a target, https://bookings.attacker.example. A named target the server does not know is still refused with invalid_target. The flag only matters when no target is named at all.
  • Check 32 already prints None in the published lab. Its server is built with require_target=False written out, so its line is identical.
  • Check 31 presents a token whose audience is the booking service. The payments service compares aud with its own name and still prints refused: wrong audience. This edit is at the authorization server and does not touch that comparison.

sections.heading: Controls
sections.html:
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

  • StandardToken exchange uses the grant type urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange. RFC 8693 section 2.1.
  • StandardImpersonation makes the actor "indistinguishable from B in that context"; delegation keeps A's own identity and records that "any actions taken are being taken by A representing B". RFC 8693 section 1.1.
  • Standardgrant_type, subject_token and subject_token_type are REQUIRED. actor_token_type "is REQUIRED when the actor_token parameter is present in the request but MUST NOT be included otherwise". RFC 8693 section 2.1.
  • Standardaudience, resource, scope and requested_token_type are OPTIONAL, and no lifetime limit is specified. RFC 8693 section 2.1.
  • StandardThe response carries access_token, issued_token_type and token_type as REQUIRED; scope is "OPTIONAL if the scope of the issued security token is identical to the scope requested by the client; otherwise, it is REQUIRED". RFC 8693 section 2.2.1.
  • Standard"If the issued token is not an access token or usable as an access token, then the token_type value N_A is used." RFC 8693 section 2.2.1.
  • StandardAn invalid request, or a subject_token or actor_token that is invalid or "unacceptable based on policy", MUST return the invalid_request error code; invalid_target SHOULD be used when the server is unwilling or unable to issue for the requested target, and "other error codes may also be used, as appropriate". RFC 8693 section 2.2.2, with the error response format and codes from RFC 6749 section 5.2.
  • Standard"The outermost act claim represents the current actor while nested act claims represent prior actors." RFC 8693 section 4.1.
  • Standard"For the purpose of applying access control policy, the consumer of a token MUST only consider the token's top-level claims and the party identified as the current actor by the act claim." RFC 8693 section 4.1.
  • StandardThe may_act claim "makes a statement that one party is authorized to become the actor and act on behalf of another party", and helps the authorization server decide whether the requested delegation is permitted. RFC 8693 section 4.4.
  • Standard"The use of the scope claim (in addition to other typical constraints such as a limited token lifetime) is suggested to mitigate potential for such abuse, as it restricts the contexts in which the delegated rights can be exercised." RFC 8693 section 5.
  • StandardLeaked or over-broad agent credentials let an agent "operate far beyond their intended scope". OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, ASI03 Identity & Privilege Abuse.
  • BaselineExchange rather than forward. A user's token does not leave the audience it was issued for.
  • BaselineSend actor_token, so the downstream decision and the audit record name the agent and the user separately.
  • BaselineRequire audience and scope on every exchange at the authorization server, rather than defaulting to the subject token's scope.
  • BaselineEnforce may_act, matched on issuer and subject together.
  • BaselineCap the issued lifetime at the subject token's remaining life.
  • BaselineAuthorize on the current actor only, and bound the depth of chains you accept.
  • BaselineLog the subject and the current actor on every delegated call.
  • OptionBind the issued token to its holder with the mechanisms in module 8 where a stolen bearer token is in the threat model.
  • OptionIssue impersonation tokens where a downstream service must not learn that an agent is involved, recording the decision and accepting that attribution is lost.
  • OptionKeep an exchange record per issued token, so a revoked session can be traced to the tokens minted from it even though it cannot recall them.

sections.heading: Review checklist items
sections.html:
These are collected into the site checklist.

  • No service forwards a user's token outside the audience it was issued for Verified by reading the outbound calls. A forwarded token carries all of the user's authority and names no agent.
  • Calls made on a user's behalf carry the user in the token, not in a parameter Otherwise the object check compares against a user ID the caller supplied.
  • Resource servers authorize on the current actor only RFC 8693 section 4.1 states it as a MUST. Test that a prior actor in a nested chain does not grant access.
  • Every exchange states audience and scope, and the server refuses without them Both are OPTIONAL in the specification. Defaulting to the subject token's scope copies everything.
  • may_act is enforced, matched on issuer and subject together A sub is unique only within an issuer. Include a same-sub, different-issuer case in the test.
  • Issued lifetimes are capped at the subject token's remaining life Nothing in RFC 8693 caps it. A revoked session cannot recall tokens already minted from it.
  • Delegation chain depth is bounded And the bound is small enough that exceeding it is a design question rather than an alert.
  • Access logs record the subject and the current actor separately An incident needs to suspend one agent without suspending the user.

<title>Four ways an agent can call a downstream service, and what each one tells it</title>

checks.title: No service forwards a user's token outside the audience it was issued for
checks.detail: Verified by reading the outbound calls. A forwarded token carries all of the user's authority and names no agent.

checks.title: Calls made on a user's behalf carry the user in the token, not in a parameter

checks.title: Resource servers authorize on the current actor only

checks.title: Every exchange states audience and scope, and the server refuses without them
checks.detail: Both are OPTIONAL in the specification. Defaulting to the subject token's scope copies everything.

checks.title: may_act is enforced, matched on issuer and subject together

details.summary: What is the protocol difference between impersonation and delegation?
details.html:
What is the protocol difference between impersonation and delegation?

One request parameter. An exchange with subject_token alone asks for impersonation, and RFC 8693 says the result is "indistinguishable from B in that context". Adding actor_token, with actor_token_type, asks for delegation, and the issued token carries an act claim naming the actor. The downstream service can then authorize the agent and attribute the action to the user.

details.summary: Your agent has its own client credentials and calls the booking API with them, passing the user's ID as a parameter. What is wrong with that?
details.html:
Your agent has its own client credentials and calls the booking API with them, passing the user's ID as a parameter. What is wrong with that?

The user is not in the token, so the booking service has nothing to compare the requested booking against. Any object check it performs is checking against a user ID supplied by the caller, which is module 9's first trap. The token's authority is also the service's, not the user's, so it is the same for every user the agent serves.

details.summary: A resource server receives a token with a nested chain of actors and finds an allowed service three levels down. May it allow the call?
details.html:
A resource server receives a token with a nested chain of actors and finds an allowed service three levels down. May it allow the call?

No. RFC 8693 section 4.1 states that for applying access control policy the consumer MUST only consider the token's top-level claims and the party identified as the current actor. Allowing on a prior actor means any service that has ever appeared in a chain can act through any service that follows it.

details.summary: You revoke a user's session. What happens to the delegated tokens already issued from it?
details.html:
You revoke a user's session. What happens to the delegated tokens already issued from it?

Nothing, unless you built something that links them. The exchange refuses to issue more, and the ones already out keep working until they expire. That is why the issued lifetime is a control rather than a detail, and why capping it at the subject token's remaining life is the starting default.
